entries.name: Alice
entries.note: The young girl protagonist of Wonderland, the dreamer and main witness, present across all twelve divisions under varied aliases (the little girl, the child, the girl, Mary Ann by mistake); her sister is a separate person and is not in this group.

entries.name: Alice's sister
entries.note: Alice's unnamed older sister, who sits on the bank with a book, wakes Alice, and dreams of Wonderland; both entries describe the same individual.

entries.name: White Rabbit
aliases: the White Rabbit with pink eyes
entries.note: The one talking white rabbit with pink eyes and a waistcoat-pocket watch, who hurries Alice down the hole, owns the house, sends for gloves and a fan, and later serves as the court's herald and reader of the verses. All six entries are this same rabbit, so they stay together in this cluster.

entries.name: Dinah
entries.note: Alice's pet cat, mentioned only and never physically present in any division; all four entries (called the cat or our cat) describe the same animal at home, so they form one cluster.

entries.name: The riverbank
entries.note: The grassy bank beside which Alice sits with her sister, where the White Rabbit runs past and where her sister dreams at sunset; both entries describe this same bank, so they form one place.

entries.name: The rabbit-hole
aliases: the large rabbit-hole under the hedge
entries.note: A deep tunnel under the hedge that dips into a long, deep well lined with cupboards and shelves. Units 3-10.

entries.name: The long low hall
entries.note: The single long, low hall with a glass table and a small door behind a curtain, where Alice grows and shrinks; the three entries are different visits to the same hall, not separate places.

entries.name: The little door to the garden
aliases: The little door and passage to the garden
entries.note: The small fifteen-inch door in the hall that leads to a passage and the garden, locked with a little golden key on a glass table; both entries describe this same door, so they belong together.

entries.name: The Mouse
entries.note: The one mouse of the Pool of Tears who swims with Alice, is offended by talk of cats and dogs, lectures on English history, tells the long tale about Fury, and storms off; the same individual in both divisions, so no other mouse in this group needs separating.

entries.name: Ada
entries.note: A girl of Alice's age whom Alice considers as a possible identity in unit 10; not present.

entries.name: Mabel
entries.note: A girl of Alice's age whom Alice considers as a possible identity in units 10 and 13; not present.

entries.name: the Duck
entries.note: The one duck in the wet gathering of birds and animals, first in the Pool of Tears swim to shore and again in the Caucus-Race, where it questions the Mouse. Both entries describe the same duck.

entries.name: the Dodo
entries.note: The Dodo, a bird who is among those fallen into the pool, swims ashore with the party, and later proposes the Caucus-race, runs it, awards the prizes and presents Alice's thimble; both entries describe the same bird.

entries.name: the Lory
entries.note: The Lory, a bird from the caucus gathering who swims ashore from the pool and later argues with Alice about age and laments the Mouse leaving; both divisions describe the same bird.

entries.name: the Eaglet
entries.note: A young eaglet among the birds that fell into the Pool of Tears and gathered on the bank for the Caucus-Race; both entries describe this same bird, so they form one cluster.

entries.name: Pool creatures
aliases: the birds and animals that had fallen into it
entries.note: The crowd of birds and animals that fell into the pool and swim together to the shore in unit 26.

entries.name: the Duchess
entries.note: The short-tempered Duchess of the kitchen, who nurses the baby and sings the lullaby, later walks with Alice, is sent away by the Queen, and is named again as the imprisoned Duchess under sentence of execution; the Pool of Tears mention is the Rabbit hurrying to her. Only one Duchess appears in this work's divisions.

entries.name: Pool of Tears
aliases: the pool of tears which she had wept
entries.note: The body of water formed from Alice's tears, where Alice swims with the Mouse and the birds and animals swim; distinct from the shore, which is the bank.

entries.name: Shore
entries.note: The shore of the pool to which Alice leads the swimming party in unit 26.

entries.name: the old Magpie
entries.note: An old magpie who wraps itself up and leaves after Alice mentions cats.

entries.name: the Canary
entries.note: A canary who calls its children away to bed after Alice mentions cats.

entries.name: the old Crab (mother of the young Crab)
entries.note: The old Crab in the Caucus race who scolds her daughter about losing her temper; told apart from the Classics master by being the mother of the young Crab in the Caucus-race section.

entries.name: the young Crab
entries.note: A young crab, daughter of the old Crab, who snaps back at her mother.

entries.name: the assembled birds and animals
entries.note: The wet gathering on the bank who sit in a ring, race, and chorus their requests as one body.

entries.name: The bank of the pool of tears
aliases: the bank of the pool of tears
entries.note: The shore of the pool of tears where the wet party assembles, dries off, holds the Caucus-Race and the Mouse's tale, and where Alice is left alone; distinct from the opening riverbank.

entries.name: Mary Ann
entries.note: The Rabbit's housemaid, only named and never seen on stage; a separate person from Alice, whom the Rabbit confuses with her.

entries.name: Pat
entries.note: The Rabbit's gardener, an Irishman (speaks with an Irish dialect) who is outside the window and handles the arm; he is heard but not seen.

entries.name: Bill the Lizard
entries.note: Bill the Lizard, the lizard sent down the chimney by the Rabbit's servants and kicked out by Alice, who later serves as a juror at the trial and writes on a slate; the three entries are one individual across divisions.

entries.name: the two guinea-pigs
entries.note: A pair of guinea-pigs who serve the Rabbit, first holding up Bill outside the house and rushing at Alice, then cheering in court until the officers bag them; no note separates them from each other, so they are kept as one pair.

entries.name: the puppy
entries.note: A large puppy in the wood that Alice plays with using a stick.

entries.name: the Caterpillar
entries.note: The large blue, languid Caterpillar smoking a hookah on a mushroom, who advises Alice in the Caterpillar sections; both entries describe this same individual, the only Caterpillar in the group.

entries.name: the White Rabbit's house
entries.note: A neat little house with a brass plate on the door; Alice grows inside its tidy room, with the stairs and window.)

entries.name: the Rabbit's garden
entries.note: The area outside the Rabbit's house where Pat, Bill and the crowd of animals gather around the window and chimney.

entries.name: The thick wood (Alice's first wood)
entries.note: The wood where Alice wanders after escaping the crowd, meets the puppy and finds the mushroom; distinct from the mushroom clearing within it and from the Duchess's woods.

entries.name: the Pigeon
entries.note: An anxious mother Pigeon in a tree nest who mistakes Alice's long neck for a serpent's and accuses her of hunting eggs.

entries.name: Father William
entries.note: The old man in Alice's recited poem who stands on his head and balances an eel; he speaks with his son, the young man, in the verses.

entries.name: the young man
entries.note: The son of Father William in Alice's recited poem, who questions his father; exists only within the poem's verses.

entries.name: The mushroom clearing
aliases: the open place in the wood
entries.note: The open clearing where the Caterpillar sits on a large round mushroom and where Alice nibbles it; a specific spot, not the wood at large.

entries.name: the treetops
entries.note: The high tree where the Pigeon has its nest, among the trees under which Alice had been wandering.

entries.name: the open place with the little house
aliases: the little house in the open place
entries.note: An open place with a small house about four feet high, which Alice approaches once she has shrunk to nine inches.

entries.name: Fish-Footman
entries.note: A footman, so called by Alice from his face, who delivers the Queen's invitation to the Duchess at the door and then sits staring at the sky; not the Frog-Footman.

entries.name: Frog-Footman
aliases: the footman with a round face and frog-like eyes
entries.note: The footman with a round face and large eyes who opens the door and repeats the invitation message; sits on the ground outside afterward.

entries.name: The Duchess's cook
entries.note: The Duchess's kitchen cook with a pepper-box, who stirs peppery soup in the kitchen scene and is later questioned about the tarts before vanishing; both entries are the same cook, linked by the kitchen, the Duchess and the pepper-box.

entries.name: Baby
entries.note: The Duchess's infant, sneezing and howling, which Alice carries outside and which turns into a pig, then runs off into the wood.

entries.name: Cheshire Cat
entries.note: The grinning cat who talks with Alice, appearing in the Duchess's kitchen and in the trees or in the air over the croquet ground and vanishing; not Dinah, who is only mentioned.

entries.name: March Hare
entries.note: The one anthropomorphic mad hare of the work, first glimpsed at his large house, then a tea-party host, then a witness at the trial; all three entries are one recurring character, distinguished only by scene.

entries.name: The Hatter
entries.note: The Mad Hatter, host of the tea-party and later first witness at the Queen's trial; the Cat's mention of a hatter living the other way is the same man, so all three entries join one cluster.

entries.name: Queen of Hearts
entries.note: The short-tempered Queen of Hearts who orders executions, runs the croquet game and sits beside the King at the trial; all six entries (including the 'Queen' who sends the croquet invitation and the 'Queen' the Hatter recalls) are the same individual, so keep them together.

entries.name: Duchess's House
entries.note: A house standing in a wood, with a door opening into a smoky kitchen where the Duchess and cook are.Alice enters the kitchen here.

entries.name: The woods around the Duchess's house
entries.note: The woods by the Duchess's house where the footmen run out, the pig escapes and the Cheshire Cat sits in a tree; tied to the Duchess's residence.

entries.name: March Hare's House
entries.note: A large house with ear-shaped chimneys and a fur-thatched roof, where the March Hare is said to live; Alice approaches it at the end.

entries.name: the Dormouse
entries.note: The sleeping Dormouse of the Mad Tea-Party, who tells the treacle-well story and is seated between the Hare and the Hatter, and also the same Dormouse who sits beside Alice and is ordered out of court in the trial; both entries are one character, distinguished only by scene.

entries.name: Time
entries.note: Personified Time, with whom the Hatter has quarrelled; mentioned only and never present on stage.

entries.name: Elsie
entries.note: One of the three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, who lived at the bottom of a treacle-well; told of, not present.

entries.name: Lacie
entries.note: One of the three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, living in the treacle-well; told of, not present.

entries.name: Tillie
entries.note: One of the three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, living in the treacle-well; told of, not present.

entries.name: Tea-table under a tree
aliases: the table in front of the house
entries.note: A large table set out under a tree in front of a house, where the tea-party takes place.

entries.name: The wood after the tea-party
entries.note: The wood Alice picks her way through after leaving the March Hare's tea-party and before the tree-door to the garden; tied to the tea-party, not the Duchess's house.

entries.name: The garden
aliases: the garden entrance by the rose-tree
entries.note: The beautiful garden of flower-beds and fountains reached through the tree-door, including its entrance by the rose-tree where the card gardeners paint the roses; the entrance is part of this same garden, not a separate place.

entries.name: Two
entries.note: One of the three card gardeners painting roses red; the one who explains the mistake to Alice. Tell him apart by his role as the spokesman; he is a playing card, not a human.

entries.name: Five
entries.note: One of the three card gardeners; blames Seven for splashing paint and warns the others of the Queen's approach. Tell him apart by his blaming of Seven and his warning; he is a playing card.

entries.name: Seven
entries.note: One of the three card gardeners; blamed by Five and the one who checks himself on seeing Alice. Tell him apart by being the one blamed by Five; he is a playing card.

entries.name: King of Hearts
entries.note: The mild, timid husband of the Queen who pardons the condemned, tries to protect Alice, and sits as judge at the trial; told apart from the Queen by his gentle, merciful conduct.

entries.name: The Knave of Hearts
entries.note: The one playing card called the Knave of Hearts, who carries the King's crown in the procession, is tried for stealing the tarts, and appears as a cardboard figure in Alice's evidence dream; all three entries are the same individual across divisions.

entries.name: The Queen's playing-card soldiers
entries.note: The ten oblong card soldiers with clubs who march in the procession, form the croquet arches, carry out the Queen's orders, and appear as the court officers who suppress the guinea-pigs and remove the Dormouse; the same card-soldier retinue in each portrayal.

entries.name: the courtiers
entries.note: Ten diamond-decorated card courtiers who walk two by two in the procession.

entries.name: the royal children
entries.note: Ten heart-decorated children who skip hand in hand in the procession.

entries.name: the executioner
entries.note: The Queen's executioner who argues about beheading the Cat and runs to fetch the Duchess in unit 70.

entries.name: the flamingo
entries.note: A live flamingo used as Alice's mallet; it twists its neck and at one point flies off into a tree.

entries.name: the hedgehogs
entries.note: Live hedgehogs used as croquet balls, which roll away and fight one another.

entries.name: the Queen's croquet-ground
entries.note: The single walled-garden croquet ground of the Queen, with flamingo mallets and hedgehog balls, where the game and executions take place; both entries describe this same place.

entries.name: the Gryphon
entries.note: A single mythical Gryphon who guides Alice to the Mock Turtle, interrupts his story, and appears again in the court; the descriptions differ in wording but depict the same creature.

entries.name: the Mock Turtle
entries.note: A sorrowful, sobbing creature with a calf's head and a turtle's tail or flappers, who tells of his schooldays in the sea, the Lobster Quadrille and the whiting, and sings 'Beautiful Soup'; the two entries are the same character across divisions, distinguished from other names in the group only by being this single individual.

entries.name: the old Turtle master (Tortoise)
entries.note: The old Turtle who taught the Mock Turtle at school under the sea; only recalled in the Mock Turtle's story, not present on stage.

entries.name: the Drawling-master (old conger-eel)
entries.note: The old conger-eel who came once a week to teach Drawling, Stretching and Fainting in Coils; recalled in the Mock Turtle's story only.

entries.name: the Classics master (old crab)
entries.note: The old crab who taught the Gryphon the Classics, recalled only in the Mock Turtle's story and never present; kept apart from the Caucus-race Crab because the notes give no sign they are the same individual.

entries.name: the rock ledge by the sea
entries.note: The lonely rock ledge where the Mock Turtle sits sobbing and tells his story, near the sea.

entries.name: the undersea school
entries.note: The school under the sea attended by the Mock Turtle in his youth, existing only in his recollection; not shown on stage.

entries.name: Whiting
entries.note: A sea fish addressed in the Mock Turtle's song; it urges a snail to join the dance. Described as the subject of the song, not a physical presence on stage.

entries.name: Snail
entries.note: A snail in the Mock Turtle's song who refuses the whiting's invitation to join the dance, saying 'Too far, too far!'.

entries.name: Porpoise
entries.note: A porpoise in the song who treads on the whiting's tail; mentioned in the whiting's explanation and in the Mock Turtle's remark about fish needing a porpoise.

entries.name: Lobsters
entries.note: Sea creatures who serve as partners in the Lobster Quadrille; they are thrown out to sea and sing of their dance in the song.

entries.name: Sea-shore
entries.note: The undersea setting where the Lobster Quadrille would be danced along the shore and where the whiting and lobsters are placed.

entries.name: Court of Justice
aliases: the court of the Queen of Hearts
entries.note: The open court of the Queen of Hearts, with throne, jury-box and table of tarts, where the trial is held; the Lobster Quadrille entry is the same court heard in the distance before it is shown on stage.

entries.name: the jury
entries.note: The twelve jurors (birds and beasts writing on slates) who act together as one body in the court; both divisions describe the same jury, so the entries are joined.

entries.name: The pack of cards (the court's playing cards)
entries.note: The playing cards of the Queen's court who rise up and fly down at Alice, ending the dream; told apart from the jury by being playing cards in the dream rather than jurors in the trial.

down-the-rabbit-hole.summary: Alice sits bored on a grassy bank beside her sister, holding a book without pictures, idly considering picking daisies while a White Rabbit with pink eyes runs close by.
The White Rabbit in a waistcoat hurries past, pulling a watch from its waistcoat-pocket, while Alice leaps to her feet and runs across the field toward the hedge where it vanishes into a rabbit-hole.
Alice dives headlong after the rabbit, tumbling down a straight tunnel-like rabbit-hole that suddenly dips into a deep well.
Alice drifts slowly down the dark well, passing cupboards, book-shelves and maps pinned on pegs, and drops an empty jar labelled ORANGE MARMALADE into a cupboard as she falls past.
Alice falls endlessly through the dark, speaking aloud and reciting distances to the centre of the earth, unsure of her latitude and longitude.
Alice falls through the dark imagining emerging among upside-down people, trying to curtsey mid-air while wondering whether the country is New Zealand or Australia.
Alice drifts drowsily through the dark, chatting about her cat Dinah and whether cats eat bats, until she lands with a thump on a heap of sticks and dry leaves.
Alice springs up unhurt and runs down a long passage after the White Rabbit, catching a glimpse of it turning a corner into a long, low hall lit by a row of hanging lamps.
Alice walks sadly down the middle of the long hall, trying every locked door along its walls and wondering how she will ever get out.
Alice finds a tiny golden key on a little three-legged glass table, then discovers a low curtain hiding a fifteen-inch door that the key fits.
Alice kneels to peer through the tiny door into a lovely garden, longing to get through but unable to fit her head, wishing she could shut up like a telescope.
Alice returns to the glass table and finds a little bottle with a paper label reading DRINK ME in large printed letters.
Alice cautiously checks the bottle for poison, recalling cautionary tales, then tastes its pleasant mixed flavour and drinks it all.
Alice feels herself shrinking, now only ten inches tall, and waits nervously beside the little door to see whether she will shrink further.
Alice finds the little golden key now out of reach on the glass table, tries to climb the slippery table leg, and sits down crying.
Alice scolds herself sharply for crying, recalling how she boxes her own ears, and reflects there is hardly enough of her left to make one respectable person.
Alice opens a little glass box under the table, finds a small cake marked EAT ME in currants, eats a bit, and checks anxiously whether she grows or shrinks.
Alice calmly finishes off the small cake on the floor beside the table, the tiny door and the golden key glinting just out of reach.

the-pool-of-tears.summary: Alice, grown very tall in the hall, looks down at her distant feet and speaks to them while planning Christmas boots.
Alice imagines sending parcels addressed to her own feet, pausing as her head bumps the roof of the hall.
Alice, nine feet tall, lies on one side peering through the tiny garden door and weeps until a pool of tears spreads across the hall.
The White Rabbit in fine clothes trots back holding gloves and a fan, then startles and runs off when Alice speaks to him.
Alice fans herself in the hot hall, puzzling over who she is, and recites lessons with a hoarse voice while sitting cross-legged.
Alice recites the crocodile verse with her hands folded in her lap, her voice sounding strange.
Alice, near tears, declares she will stay below, then notices she is wearing one of the Rabbit's white gloves and is shrinking beside the table.
Small Alice stands by the shut little door and the golden key on the glass table, relieved but dismayed.
Alice slips and splashes into salty water up to her chin, thinking of the seaside and bathing machines.
Alice swims in the pool of tears, lamenting that she may drown in her own weeping.
Alice swims toward a small splashing creature, then addresses the Mouse in the pool with a formal greeting.
Alice speaks French to the Mouse, which leaps out of the water in fright at the mention of cats.
Alice praises her cat Dinah while the bristling Mouse swims away, offended, insisting its family hated cats.
Alice describes a farmer's terrier to the Mouse, which swims off in anger, then turns back pale and agrees to tell its history on shore.
A crowd of a Duck, a Dodo, a Lory, an Eaglet and other creatures swims in the pool as Alice leads them toward the shore.

a-caucus-race-and-a-long-tale.summary: The dripping, cross birds and animals gather on the bank in a ring while the Mouse, in the middle, calls for everyone to sit and promises to make them dry.
The Mouse, seated among the assembled creatures, begins reading a dry history lesson aloud while the Lory shivers and the Mouse frowns at interruptions.
The Duck, Mouse, Alice, Dodo and eaglet bicker in the circle over the history passage, and the Dodo proposes a Caucus-race as the cure for being wet.
Alice asks what a Caucus-race is and the Dodo marks out a circular course where the creatures run freely, stopping when they are dry.
The panting creatures crowd round the Dodo, who pronounces everyone a winner, and they turn to Alice to hand out prizes from her pocket of comfits.
Alice produces her thimble as a prize and the creatures gather solemnly round her as the Dodo presents it while she bows with a straight face.
The creatures eat their comfits amid choking and fuss, then sit in a ring as the Mouse begins its tale, and Alice imagines the long tail as the verse of the Mouse's story.
Alice, distracted and mishearing 'bend' as 'knot', upsets the Mouse, who stands and walks away while Alice apologises.
Alice calls after the departing Mouse as the Lory sighs and the Crabs bicker, and Alice explains her cat Dinah to the Lory.
The birds scatter in alarm at the mention of a cat that hunts birds, and Alice sits alone and weeping, then looks up hoping to see the Mouse return.

the-rabbit-sends-in-a-little-bill.summary: A hurried white rabbit trots back along a strange hall, peering anxiously at the ground while Alice watches, searching for lost gloves and a fan.
The rabbit barks orders at Alice, mistaking her for a housemaid; she runs toward a small neat house with a brass plate reading W. RABBIT and hurries inside and upstairs.
In a tidy room with a table in the window, Alice takes a fan and gloves, then drinks from an unlabelled bottle and begins to swell until her head presses the ceiling.
Alice, now huge and cramped, kneels and lies in the small room with one arm out the window and her foot up the chimney, lamenting her plight.
Alice sits crammed in the small room talking to herself about whether she will ever grow older and about lessons, arguing with her own reflection.
The rabbit comes up the stairs and tries the door, which is blocked by Alice's pressed elbow, so it goes off to try the window.
Alice snatches at the air outside the window and the rabbit falls with a crash of glass; the rabbit calls for Pat, who is outside and confused.
Pat stands below the window staring at Alice's arm filling the window frame while the rabbit scolds him, and Alice snatches again, causing more shrieks and breaking glass.
A crowd of servants hauls ladders and rope onto the roof, and they argue over who must go down the chimney; Alice, trying to be brave, kicks her foot as a small animal scrambles near her.
Bill the lizard is shot out of the chimney like a sky-rocket and lies dazed while the others crowd around holding his head and giving him brandy.
The rabbit's crowd threatens to burn the house down, Alice threatens to set Dinah on them, and a dead silence falls as they plan to start with a barrowful of something.
Pebbles rattle through the window and turn into small cakes; Alice eats one and shrinks, then bursts out of the house into a crowd of animals and birds tending the lizard Bill.
Alice wanders in a thick wood and meets a huge puppy, which she teases with a stick, running around a thistle as it charges and tumbles before it finally sits panting.
Alice escapes the puppy, rests against a buttercup and fans herself, wondering how to grow back to her proper size and what to eat or drink.
Alice peers over the top of a large mushroom and meets the gaze of a big blue caterpillar sitting with folded arms, smoking a long hookah.

advice-from-a-caterpillar.summary: On a mushroom, the languid Caterpillar with its hookah eyes Alice as she tries to explain that she is no longer herself.
Alice and the Caterpillar bicker in short exchanges; Alice turns to leave, is called back, and the Caterpillar sits puffing on its hookah while she waits.
Alice, standing before the seated Caterpillar, recites Father William's poem in a melancholy voice while the Caterpillar listens.
The Caterpillar asks what size Alice wants and rears up to its full three inches, angrily dismissing her complaint as it returns to smoking.
The Caterpillar crawls off through the grass, and Alice stands by the round mushroom trying to tell which side is which.
Alice nibbles the mushroom, strikes her foot with her chin, then finds her shoulders gone and her neck rising like a stalk above a sea of green treetops.
A large Pigeon flaps at Alice's face in a nest among the treetops, shouting that she is a serpent while Alice protests and they argue about eggs.
Alice crouches among the branches, nibbles the mushroom pieces to return to her normal height, and approaches a small house about four feet high.

pig-and-pepper.summary: A footman in livery runs out of the wood toward a house, while Alice watches from the trees.
The Fish-Footman hands a large letter to the Frog-Footman, bowing so their curls tangle; Alice laughs and hides in the wood, then sees the Fish-Footman gone and the other sitting staring at the sky.
Alice knocks at the door; the Footman sitting outside, eyes fixed on the sky, says knocking is pointless and ignores her question about getting in.
A plate flies from the doorway past the Footman's nose and shatters on a tree while he rambles on about sitting there till tomorrow, and Alice repeats her question.
Alice grumbles to herself about argumentative creatures, the Footman whistles, and she gives up on him and goes into the house.
Alice enters a smoky kitchen where the Duchess sits on a stool nursing a baby, the cook stirs a cauldron of peppery soup, and a grinning Cheshire cat lies by the hearth.
Alice asks the Duchess why the cat grins; the Duchess snaps at the baby and makes a curt remark about Alice knowing little, as the cook prepares to hurl things.
The cook flings fire-irons, saucepans and dishes at the Duchess and baby while Alice jumps in terror; the Duchess growls that the world would spin faster if everyone minded their business.
Alice lectures on the earth's rotation as the Duchess calls for someone's head to be chopped off, then the Duchess sings to the baby, tossing it up and down.
The Duchess sings her pepper-and-sneezing lullaby verses while the cook and baby join in with howls, the baby bouncing violently in her arms.
The Duchess thrusts the baby at Alice and runs out to play croquet; Alice struggles to hold the squirming, star-fish-like infant.
Alice carries the baby outdoors, knotted up and gripping its ear and foot, and scolds its grunting as its nose turns snout-like and its eyes shrink.
Alice finds the baby has become a pig, sets it down, and watches it trot into the wood, then notices the Cheshire Cat grinning on a branch.
Alice politely addresses the Cheshire Cat sitting in a tree, which grins at her and answers that the direction depends on where she wants to go.
The Cat points one paw toward a Hatter and the other toward a March Hare, declares everyone there mad, and argues Alice must be mad too.
The Cat explains madness through growling and purring dogs and vanishes, promising to see Alice at the croquet game.
The Cat reappears, asks what became of the baby, and vanishes again after Alice says it turned into a pig.
Alice walks on toward the March Hare, where the Cat reappears on a branch, asks whether she said pig or fig, and slowly vanishes leaving only its grin floating in the tree.
Alice, shrunk to about two feet, approaches the large March Hare's house with ear-shaped chimneys and fur thatch, nervously wondering whether its occupant is raving mad.

a-mad-tea-party.summary: Alice sits down at a crowded tea table under a tree, where the March Hare and Hatter lean on the sleeping Dormouse, and she bristles at the rude 'No room' and the mocked offer of wine.
Alice argues with the Hatter over her hair and manners while he asks the raven-and-writing-desk riddle, and she eagerly declares she can guess it.
At the tea table the three debate whether 'I see what I eat' equals 'I eat what I see', the Dormouse muttering in his sleep, and the party falls silent with Alice puzzling over ravens and desks.
The Hatter checks his broken watch and asks the date while the March Hare dips it in tea, and Alice remarks on the watch that tells the day but not the hour.
The Hatter pours hot tea on the Dormouse's nose, admits no answer to the riddle, and explains that Time won't be beaten, so he and the Hare stay stuck at teatime.
The Hatter recounts the Queen's concert where he sang 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat' and was ordered beheaded for murdering the time, so now it is always six o'clock.
Alice asks why there are so many tea-things and learns the cups are moved round the table, and she asks what happens when they reach the beginning again.
The March Hare asks Alice to tell a story, and they pinch the Dormouse awake to tell one instead, the Dormouse yawning as the Hatter threatens to fall asleep again.
The Dormouse begins the tale of three sisters who lived at the bottom of a treacle-well, and Alice objects to the diet and the location while the Hatter offers her more tea.
The Dormouse insists the well was made of treacle and is scolded for sulking, then the company shuffles places so the Hatter gains a clean cup and the milk-jug spills into the Hare's plate.
Alice asks where the treacle was drawn from, and the Hatter jokes about drawing water from a well while the bewildered Alice lets the Dormouse continue.
The Dormouse, nodding off and pinched awake by the Hatter, rambles about drawing everything beginning with M, including muchness, and the Hatter snaps at Alice to stop talking.
Disgusted, Alice storms off through the wood while the Hare and Hatter ignore her and try to stuff the sleeping Dormouse into the teapot.
Alice vows never to return, then spots a door in a tree trunk, unlocks it with the golden key, nibbles the mushroom to shrink, and steps into the bright garden with its flower-beds and fountains.

the-queens-croquet-ground.summary: Alice stands at a rose-tree in the garden as three painting gardeners, Two, Five and Seven, argue over spilled red paint.
The gardeners bicker and then freeze as they notice Alice watching them, all bowing low to her.
Alice asks why they are painting the roses; Two explains the wrong tree, and Five cries out that the Queen is coming, so the gardeners throw themselves flat.
The royal procession passes: soldiers with clubs, courtiers with diamonds, royal children with hearts, the White Rabbit, the Knave with the crown, and the King and Queen of Hearts.
Alice stands upright while the Queen questions her, demands the gardeners be identified, and screams for Alice's head until Alice declares nonsense loudly.
The King calms the Queen, the gardeners rise and bow, the Queen condemns them, and Alice hides the gardeners in a flower-pot as soldiers search for them.
The Queen asks whether the gardeners' heads are off, asks Alice if she plays croquet, and Alice joins the procession.
Walking beside the anxious White Rabbit, Alice is whispered to about the Duchess being under sentence of execution for boxing the Queen's ears.
The Queen shouts for everyone to take their places; the croquet-ground of ridges and furrows, hedgehog balls, flamingo mallets and doubled-up soldiers arches is set, and Alice grows uneasy.
Alice spots a grinning Cheshire Cat floating in the air and begins describing the chaotic game to its emerging head.
Alice speaks dismissively of the Queen while the Queen stands listening close behind, then the Queen smiles and passes on.
The King inspects the Cat, hides behind Alice, orders it removed, and the Queen calls for a beheading; the King runs off for the executioner while Alice goes back to find her hedgehog.
Alice chases her escaped flamingo across the garden and brings it back, finding the hedgehogs gone.
Alice returns to a crowd around the Cat where the executioner, King and Queen argue loudly over whether a head can be cut off without a body.
Alice suggests asking the Duchess; the Queen sends for her, and as the executioner hurries off the Cat's head vanishes, leaving the King and executioner searching while the others return to the game.

the-mock-turtles-story.summary: Alice strolls arm in arm with the Duchess, who is in an unexpectedly cheerful mood, as they walk away together through the garden.
Alice ponders aloud to herself about pepper and temper while the Duchess, having drifted off, startles Alice by speaking close to her ear.
Alice and the Duchess walk close together, the Duchess's sharp chin digging into Alice's shoulder as she offers morals about the game and love making the world go round.
Alice, uneasy, is nearly touched by the Duchess's flamingo and mustard talk while the Duchess chatters on about birds, minerals and a mustard-mine.
Alice identifies mustard as a vegetable while the Duchess delivers a tangled moral; Alice privately thinks the gift of talk is a cheap present.
The Duchess presses her chin into Alice and begins another sentence, then freezes as the Queen appears before them with folded arms, scowling like a thunderstorm.
The Duchess, cowering, greets the Queen weakly while the Queen stamps and orders her off with her head or the Duchess herself; the Duchess flees instantly.
The croquet-ground is crowded with frightened players and soldiers making arches, the Queen shouting death sentences as her victims are dragged away into custody.
Out of breath, the Queen asks Alice about the Mock Turtle, and they set off together across the grounds.
As the Queen walks away, the King quietly pardons all the condemned players while Alice walks beside the Queen.
A sleeping Gryphon is roused by the Queen, who sends Alice off with it; the Gryphon chuckles at the Queen's fancy and Alice wanders on after it.
Alice and the Gryphon approach the Mock Turtle sitting sadly on a rocky ledge, weeping, and sit down to hear his history.
The Mock Turtle pauses in a long silence, sobbing and sighing, as he begins by saying he was once a real Turtle.
The Mock Turtle recalls school in the sea with its Tortoise master while Alice is scolded by the Mock Turtle and Gryphon for questioning him.
The Mock Turtle insists they went to school in the sea and Alice interrupts, both sides of their schooling sparring over day-school and extras.
Alice and the Mock Turtle compare school bills, French, music and washing, while Alice remarks on the odd idea of learning at the bottom of the sea.
The Mock Turtle describes the regular course of Reeling, Writhing and Arithmetic while the Gryphon lifts its paws at Alice's ignorance of uglifying.
The Gryphon scolds Alice as a simpleton while the Mock Turtle counts subjects on his flappers, and both creatures hide their faces in their paws over Laughing and Grief.
Alice asks about the hours of lessons; the Gryphon explains lessons lessen each day, and the Mock Turtle is told to move on to the games.

the-lobster-quadrille.summary: The weeping Mock Turtle sobs with a flapper across his eyes while the Gryphon pats his back; Alice sits listening, asking what the Lobster Quadrille is.
The Gryphon and Mock Turtle leap about wildly on the shore, shouting the dance steps at each other, then slump down sadly while Alice watches.
The two creatures dance solemnly around Alice, treading on her toes, while the Mock Turtle sings the whiting and snail song.
Alice and the Mock Turtle talk at the shore about whitings, with the Mock Turtle yawning and the Gryphon explaining their tails in their mouths.
The Gryphon explains why whitings do the boots and shoes under the sea while Alice listens, puzzled, with the porpoise and fish in the background.
Alice explains her adventures to the Gryphon and Mock Turtle, who sit close on each side of her, staring with wide eyes and mouths.
Alice stands reciting the garbled verse about the Lobster while the Gryphon and Mock Turtle frown and question her, her head full of the dance.
Alice recites the Owl and Panther verses while the Mock Turtle interrupts her, and she sits down with her face in her hands.
The Gryphon asks Alice to pick a song, and the Mock Turtle sings Beautiful Soup with sobs while the Gryphon calls for a chorus.
Alice and the Gryphon run hand in hand over the shore toward the distant trial as the Mock Turtle's song fades behind them.

who-stole-the-tarts.summary: The King and Queen of Hearts sit on their throne amid a crowd of birds, beasts and cards, the Knave in chains between two soldiers, the White Rabbit with trumpet and scroll, and a table of tarts in the middle of the court where Alice eyes them hungrily.
Alice, at the trial, looks around and recognises the judge in his wig, the King wearing his crown over it, and the jury-box holding twelve creatures.
The jurors scribble on slates while Alice whispers to the Gryphon; Alice sneaks up behind the lizard juror Bill and snatches his squeaking pencil.
The White Rabbit blows his trumpet and reads the verse about the Knave stealing the tarts before the King, the jury and the Rabbit, and calls the first witness.
The nervous Hatter enters with a teacup and bread-and-butter, is questioned by the King about dates with the March Hare and Dormouse, and the Queen stares at him as he bites his teacup.
Alice grows larger and crowds the Dormouse beside her, who protests and sulkily moves to the other side of the court.
The Queen glares at the trembling Hatter, who shakes off his shoes while testifying about the twinkling tea, interrupted by the March Hare and the sleeping Dormouse.
The Hatter kneels, the guinea-pigs are suppressed in a canvas bag, and the Hatter is dismissed; he runs out barefoot while the Queen orders his head taken off.
The Duchess's cook arrives carrying a pepper-box, making people sneeze, and the King, folding his arms, begins to cross-examine her about what tarts are made of.
The cook answers pepper, the sleepy Dormouse says treacle, the Queen shrieks for him to be seized and removed, and the cook vanishes during the commotion.
Alice, waiting in the court, is startled as the White Rabbit shrilly calls out her own name as the next witness.

alices-evidence.summary: Alice, large and flustered, has knocked over the jury-box, spilling jurymen onto the crowd in the court; she gathers them up and sets the Lizard upright in the box while the King demands all jurymen return to their places.

In the courtroom, the jury hurriedly writes out a history of the accident while the Lizard gapes at the roof; the King questions Alice, who knows nothing, and the White Rabbit whispers a correction to the King's wording.

Alice stands defiantly before the King, Queen and jury as the King reads out a rule to expel those over a mile high, and Alice retorts that it is a rule he has just invented; the King turns pale and shuts his book.
The White Rabbit, flustered, holds up a folded paper with no name or address on it, unfolding it to reveal a set of verses; the Queen, King and jury look on as the Knave stands nearby.
The jurymen puzzle over the handwriting and the King speculates about imitation, while the Knave protests his innocence; the White Rabbit puts on spectacles and prepares to read the verses aloud.
The White Rabbit reads the rhyming verses aloud to the assembled court, with the King, Queen, jury and Knave listening attentively.

The King rubs his hands over the verses while Alice declares she sees no meaning in them and offers sixpence; the King peers at the paper with one eye while the Knave, made of cardboard, shakes his head.

The King, pointing at the tarts on the table, interprets the verses while the Queen furiously throws an inkstand at the Lizard, who keeps writing with ink dripping down his face; the court falls silent.

The King takes offence at his own pun and the court laughs; the Queen demands sentence first, Alice protests, and the Queen shouts for Alice's head as Alice, now full-size, calls the courtroom a pack of cards.
The whole pack of cards rises and swoops down on Alice, who screams and flails, and she wakes on the riverbank with her sister brushing dead leaves from her face, then tells her sister her dream.

Alice runs home to tea while her sister sits on the bank at sunset, dreaming of Alice and the creatures of Wonderland—the rabbit, the Mouse, the March Hare, the Queen, the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle—before imagining Alice grown into a woman telling children stories.

brief.tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling undercurrent of childish bewilderment that shifts toward sharp absurdity in the courtroom and softer melancholy by the river at the close.

depictionRules.text: Alice's changing size must always read clearly against furniture, doors, trees and other figures.
Animals are talking characters with human posture and dress where the text gives it; the birds keep their feathers and the Mouse its tail.
Playing-card courtiers and soldiers are flat, oblong card figures with suits visible on their bodies.
Violence and executions are only threatened or shown as slapstick; no gore or real injury is depicted.
Dinah, the Duchess (outside her scene), Ada and Mabel remain mentioned only and are never drawn on stage.
The Mock Turtle has a calf's head and turtle-shell tail; the Gryphon has a lion's body and eagle's head and wings.

eras.label: Victorian England, dreamlike underground Wonderland
eras.people: Alice, a young English girl, alongside talking animals and playing-card courtiers; her sister appears only on the riverbank at the start and end.
eras.dress: Victorian pinafore dresses, white blouses, stockings and boots for Alice; formal court robes and card-pattern costumes for the royals.
eras.buildingsAndObjects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, glass table, small key, labelled bottle, cake, mushroom, pool of tears, croquet-ground, courtroom with jury-box and tarts.
eras.technology: Pocket watches, slates, pencils and printed labels exist; oil lamps only, no machines, no modern vehicles or devices.

styleReasons.reason: Ink lines and transparent washes suit the whimsical, damp and intimate dreamlike scenes of falling, swimming and shrinking.
Dramatic light and painterly scale suit the courtroom, the croquet-ground and the grand hall of the Queen's court.

raw.tone: Whimsical and dreamlike, with a gently unsettling undercurrent of childish bewilderment that shifts toward sharp absurdity in the courtroom and softer melancholy by the river at the close.
depiction_rules: Alice's changing size must always read clearly against furniture, doors, trees and other figures.
Animals are talking characters with human posture and dress where the text gives it; the birds keep their feathers and the Mouse its tail.
Playing-card courtiers and soldiers are flat, oblong card figures with suits visible on their bodies.
Violence and executions are only threatened or shown as slapstick; no gore or real injury is depicted.
Dinah, the Duchess (outside her scene), Ada and Mabel remain mentioned only and are never drawn on stage.
The Mock Turtle has a calf's head and turtle-shell tail; the Gryphon has a lion's body and eagle's head and wings.

eras.name: Victorian England, dreamlike underground Wonderland
eras.people: Alice, a young English girl, alongside talking animals and playing-card courtiers; her sister appears only on the riverbank at the start and end.
eras.dress: Victorian pinafore dresses, white blouses, stockings and boots for Alice; formal court robes and card-pattern costumes for the royals.
eras.buildings_and_objects: Riverbank, rabbit-hole, long hall, glass table, small key, labelled bottle, cake, mushroom, pool of tears, croquet-ground, courtroom with jury-box and tarts.
eras.technology: Pocket watches, slates, pencils and printed labels exist; oil lamps only, no machines, no modern vehicles or devices.
